briefFidelity: FAIL, and the failure is an inversion rather than an absence. The brief pairs the poles explicitly in one sentence: stress = sparse, broken and COLD (slate and iron); recovery = dense, whole and WARM (ochre and copper). The work delivers the density axis correctly and the temperature axis exactly backwards. In my pre-brief description, written without having read a word of this, I recorded 'STRESS disperses and HEATS' and 'RECOVERY ... the amber recedes and greys down'. That is the finding. On the sheet: 9011 neutral carries one small amber lozenge, 9011 stress carries three saturated amber elements (square upper-right, diamond mid-left, bright parallelogram lower-left), and 9011 recovery is nearly monochrome slate with the amber reduced to a dim smear. 9548 stress promotes ochre to a large saturated block across the top plus a lower-right slab, while 9548 recovery buries it under grey. 9190 stress gains three amber elements; 9190 recovery keeps only a small knot at centre. 9369 stress adds a second amber slab at the bottom and is the most saturated of its three. So the hue ramp runs recovery(coldest) < neutral < stress(warmest) - monotonic, legible, and the reverse of what was commissioned. Under drawdown this collection glows copper; in recovery it goes to iron. A second, smaller miss: 'Neutral sits visibly between them' does not hold on the density axis, where neutral and recovery are near-twins (compare 9011 neutral against 9011 recovery, or 9548 neutral against 9548 recovery - both pairs are consolidated stacks) and stress is the lone outlier, so the three states read as two, not as a ramp. This is a gate and it is not close.
composition: Inconsistent by seed rather than by intent, and the frame is never used. All twelve are centred clusters floating in a square with a wide dead margin on all four sides; nothing is anchored to an edge, cropped by it, or in any relationship with it. Only 9369 approaches the frame. Focal hierarchy exists in three seeds - 9369 (big amber square under a notched slate slab), 10622 (amber rectangle between large slate squares) and 10801 (monolithic slate mass) genuinely read as figure on ground. Five more (9011, 9727, 10085, 10264, 9548) are mid-density piles with a soft centre of gravity but nothing that commands the frame. Three (9190, 10443, 10980) are even fields of small incident with no dominant element at all - debris with a hole in the middle. The brief's 'weathers over the same terrain' wants terrain; there is no terrain here, only a floating blob in the middle of black.
collectionCoherence: The strongest axis, and genuinely good. Laid out together these unmistakably read as one project: one ground, one two-hue palette, one alpha-stacking logic, one rotated-square-and-disc vocabulary, one centred-cluster placement rule. There is no seed on the 12-up sheet that looks imported from another system. 9906 is the nearest to an outlier - dominated by two large pale discs with almost no amber - and even it stays clearly inside the family. If anything the coherence is slightly too tight: it is bought by every token obeying the same composition rule rather than by a shared sensibility surviving different compositional decisions.
palette: Chosen, restrained and legible - slate blue-grey against amber/ochre on near-black - and it is the only reason the state change is visible at 120px at all. Contrast range does real work in 9369, 10622 and 10085 where a single warm element carries the eye. Two complaints. First, the alpha stacking manufactures a third colour nobody chose: amber at low opacity over near-black yields a dead tobacco brown, plainly visible bottom-left of 9369 neutral and at the left of 9727, and where six or more shapes cross in 9548 and 10264 the result is an indeterminate muddy olive that reads as accident rather than construction. Second, and decisively, the palette's two poles are correctly identified as the brief's slate/iron and ochre/copper but are wired to the wrong states.
seedVariation: Adequate in range, thin in kind. The twelve are not one work at twelve rotations - the gap between 10443 (near-empty scatter) and 9369 (near-full amber field) is genuinely wide, and 9906's disc-dominance is a real alternative. But the variation is quantitative: three dials move - element count, element scale, and how much amber is permitted - and nothing structural varies. No seed invents a different arrangement, a different relationship to the frame, or a different compositional strategy. 9011, 9727, 10085 and 10264 sit close enough to read as four shuffles of one deck. This is not a failure in either direction the axis names; it is a system with less invention than its own element vocabulary could support.
thumbnailSurvival: Mixed, and it splits the collection into thirds. The seeds with one big mass and strong hue contrast hold cleanly at 120 - 9369, 10622, 10801 and 9906 are all still readable objects. The dense seeds lose their interior: 9548, 10264 and 9727 collapse into a grey smudge with an orange smear, and comparing against the 256 sheet confirms this is real loss rather than my eye, since at 256 the squares in 9548 are countable and at 120 they are not. The sparse seeds fail the other way: 10443 at 120 is a few grey specks in a black square and barely reads as an artwork, with 10980 close behind. Twelve tokens at 120 still look like more than three or four distinct things, so the sheet passes the bare test, but the middle-density group blurs toward one another. Crucially for this brief, the state change DOES survive at 120 - stress's detached satellites and hotter amber and recovery's greying are both visible on the 120 states sheet. The transformation is delivered at browse size. It is delivered pointing the wrong way.
marketResponse: Visible, consistent in direction across all four seeds shown, and wrong. The change is real and not a bytes-only transition: stress spreads the cluster, detaches discrete circles and diamonds as drifting satellites (9011 stress gains a disc at top-left and diamonds lower-left; 9548 stress gains discs off to the right; 9190 stress scatters throughout), and increases rotation - that half is the 'sparse and broken' the brief asked for. Recovery consolidates into a flatter, more overlapped, whole stack - again correct. But the thermal half runs backwards on every seed: stress is the warmest and most saturated row (9548 stress's big top block, 9369 stress's second amber slab, 9011 stress's three amber elements), recovery is the coldest and greyest (9011 recovery near-monochrome, 9548 recovery's amber buried under slate). The claimed change is 'cold under drawdown, warm in recovery'. The delivered change is the opposite. A state transition that is visible but inverted has not been delivered; it has been contradicted.
tokenIdentity: The best-executed requirement in the brief, and it is executed well. Each seed remains itself across all three states: 9190 is a scatter of small squares around a pale disc in neutral, stress and recovery alike; 9369 is 'big amber square plus notched slate slab' in all three; 9011 is a leaning mid-scale stack in all three. Scale class, element-count class and rough placement all persist, so nothing here has been replaced by another work under drawdown. 9548 travels furthest - its amber migrates from mid-right in neutral to a dominant block at the top in stress - and even that keeps the dense-pile character intact. If the brief has a tension between 'almost unrecognisable' and 'same token', this work resolves it firmly toward identity, which is the safer of the two errors and is not what I am refusing it for.
artifacts: No hard technical faults: I see no clipping at the viewBox, no shape halved by the frame, no vanished stroke, nothing that reads as a rendering bug. The flaws are compositional. Alpha stacking produces muddy indeterminate mid-tones wherever six or more shapes cross - the centre of 9548 and 10264 in every state, and 9727 - so the overlaps read as pile-up rather than as construction. The amber-over-black brown at the bottom-left of 9369 neutral and the left of 9727 is a dead dirty colour that neither chosen hue asked for. The small detached squares at the lower-left of 10264 and scattered through 9190 and 10443 read as leftovers rather than placed elements. 9548 stress pushes its amber block close enough to the top of its tile to look crowded, though not cut.
reasoning: REFUSE, on the gate, and one sentence decides it: the brief asks for stress to be cold slate and iron and recovery to be warm ochre and copper, and this work does the exact opposite on every seed shown. I am confident in that finding because I wrote it down before I read the brief - my Stage 1 description independently recorded stress as the row that 'disperses and HEATS' and recovery as the row where 'the amber recedes and greys down', which is the inverse of the commission in language I had no way to have borrowed. This is not a near miss or a matter of degree. The work clearly understood that it was being asked for a two-axis transformation and it built one: the density axis is right (stress sparse and broken, recovery dense and whole), the market response is genuinely visible at 120px, and token identity is preserved cleanly across all three states, which is the requirement most submissions fail. It got the harder half right. But it wired the thermal axis backwards, so the collection glows copper under drawdown and turns to iron in recovery, which reverses the meaning of the piece - the market is the subject, and this one says the wrong thing about the market in the most legible channel it has. A secondary miss compounds it: neutral does not sit visibly between the other two on density, where neutral and recovery are near-twins and stress is a lone outlier, so three states read as two. I am not refusing this for being a different artwork than the one commissioned - the vocabulary, the coherence and the identity discipline are all answering this brief and answering it competently. I am refusing it because on the single axis the brief spends most of its words specifying, the sign is flipped, and that is not something a viewer can be asked to read past on a permanent on-chain commit.
wouldChange: One change is decisive and mechanical: swap the thermal polarity so stress drives toward slate and iron and recovery drives toward ochre and copper, leaving the density behaviour exactly as it is. That single sign flip would take 9011 stress from three saturated amber elements to a cold desaturated scatter and would let 9011 recovery close warm instead of near-monochrome, and it would make the brief's sentence true on all four state seeds without touching the composition engine. Second, separate neutral from recovery on density so the ramp reads as three points rather than as stress-versus-everything - 9011 and 9548 currently show neutral and recovery as near-twins, so give recovery meaningfully more overlap and consolidation than neutral has. Third, put a floor and a ceiling on element count: 10443 and 10980 have too little on the ground to read at 120px, and 9548, 10264 and 9727 have enough crossing shapes that the centre turns to indeterminate mud - capping the stack depth at any point would also kill the dead tobacco-brown that amber-over-black is producing at the bottom-left of 9369. Fourth, and optional but worth it, let something meet the frame: every one of the twelve floats in a wide black margin, and the brief's 'terrain' has no ground plane for a weather to sit on.
